t: The Sogdians, an Iranian people of the Zeravshan and Kashka Darya valleys in present-day Uzbekistan and Tajikistan, lived in oasis city-states such as Samarkand, Bukhara and Panjikent.
From the 4th to the 8th century CE their merchants dominated the trade between Central Asia and China, settling from the Tarim Basin to the Tang capital and serving Turkic and Chinese rulers.
Conquered by the Arabs in the early 8th century, they became Muslim and Persian- or Turkic-speaking, but their alphabet lives on, through the Uyghurs, in the Mongolian script.
dyk: A Tang history claims that Sogdian parents put honey or sugar in a newborn son’s mouth and glue in his palm, so that he would grow up to speak sweet words and to hold on to money.
ev: Cyrus the Great brings Sogdiana into the Achaemenid Empire
Alexander the Great conquers Sogdiana despite the resistance led by Spitamenes
Sogdian merchants in China write the Ancient Letters, found near Dunhuang in 1907
The Sogdian Maniakh leads a Turkic embassy to the emperor Justin II in Constantinople
The hall of the ambassadors at Afrasiab is painted for Varkhuman, king of Samarkand
The Arabs under Qutayba ibn Muslim take Samarkand
The An Lushan Rebellion, led by a general of Sogdian and Turkic parentage, shakes the Tang Dynasty
Under the Samanids the Sogdians become Muslim and come to speak Persian

f.homeland: Sogdiana, between the Amu Darya and Syr Darya rivers, chiefly the valleys of the Zeravshan and the Kashka Darya (present-day Uzbekistan and Tajikistan), with merchant colonies from the Tarim Basin and Mongolia to the cities of northern China
f.period: c. 6th century BCE, when Sogdiana appears in Persian inscriptions, to about the 11th century CE, by which time its people had become Muslim and spoke Persian or Turkic; its trade at its height in the 4th–8th centuries CE
f.known: Silk Road merchants and their colonies in China; city-states such as Samarkand, Bukhara and Panjikent; wall paintings of epics, feasts and embassies; an alphabet that passed to the Uyghurs, Mongols and Manchus; musicians and dancers at the Tang court
f.sources: Sogdian documents (the Ancient Letters, the Mount Mugh archive, Buddhist, Manichaean and Christian texts from Dunhuang and Turfan, the Bugut inscription); excavations at Panjikent, Afrasiab and Varakhsha; Sogdian tombs in China; Persian, Greek, Chinese, Byzantine and Arabic accounts
